items.stem: A Pigouvian tax is designed to
options: make the polluter pay a tax equal to the marginal external cost at the social optimum
raise as much revenue as possible
reduce the price paid by consumers
subsidise producers of merit goods
items.answer: make the polluter pay a tax equal to the marginal external cost at the social optimum
items.markingKey: Internalises the externality: MPC + tax = MSC.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain how an indirect tax can correct a negative production externality.
items.answer: Diagram: MPC below MSC by MEC; demand = MSB. Market output Q1 where MPC = MSB. A tax equal to MEC at Q* shifts MPC up to MSC (MPC + tax), so output falls to Q* where MSC = MSB and price rises; the welfare loss triangle is removed and tax revenue is raised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: curves; 1 mark: tax shifts supply up by MEC; 1 mark: new output Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss eliminated [4]

items.stem: Explain two problems a government faces in setting the correct tax on pollution.
items.answer: Difficulty measuring the marginal external cost; MEC varies by location and time; inelastic demand means output falls little; political pressure; firms may relocate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: In the market for sugary drinks, demand is Qd = 430 − 2P and supply is Qs = 355 + 3P (Q in thousand units, P in $). The government imposes a specific tax of $10 per unit on producers. Calculate the equilibrium price before the tax.

In the market for airline tickets, demand is Qd = 230 − 2P and supply is Qs = 155 + 3P (Q in thousand units, P in $). The government imposes a specific tax of $10 per unit on producers. Calculate the equilibrium before the tax, the price paid by consumers and received by producers after the tax, the tax revenue and the share of the tax borne by consumers.
items.answer: Before: P = $15, Q = 200 thousand. After: consumers pay $21, producers receive $11, Q = 188 thousand; revenue = $1880 thousand; consumers bear 60%.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium 230 − 2P = 155 + 3P → P = 15, Q = 200 [1]. With tax supply: Qs = 155 + 3(P − 10); 230 − 2P = 125 + 3P → P = 21 [1]; producer price 11 [1]; Q = 188; revenue = 10 × 188 = 1880 [1]; consumer share = (21 − 15)/10 = 60% [1].

items.stem: In the market for sugary drinks, demand is Qd = 245 − 3P and supply is Qs = 170 + 2P (Q in thousand units, P in $). The government imposes a specific tax of $10 per unit on producers. Calculate the equilibrium before the tax, the price paid by consumers and received by producers after the tax, the tax revenue and the share of the tax borne by consumers.
items.answer: Before: P = $15, Q = 200 thousand. After: consumers pay $19, producers receive $9, Q = 188 thousand; revenue = $1880 thousand; consumers bear 40%.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium 245 − 3P = 170 + 2P → P = 15, Q = 200 [1]. With tax supply: Qs = 170 + 2(P − 10); 245 − 3P = 150 + 2P → P = 19 [1]; producer price 9 [1]; Q = 188; revenue = 10 × 188 = 1880 [1]; consumer share = (19 − 15)/10 = 40% [1].

items.stem: Extract: Scientists estimate the marginal external cost of carbon emissions in Westaria at $60 per tonne. The government is debating a carbon tax of $20 per tonne, a cap-and-trade permit scheme, or stricter regulation of power stations. (a) Explain whether the proposed tax is likely to achieve the social optimum. (b) Explain one way in which this intervention could lead to government failure.
items.answer: (a) Tax below MEC: output still above the optimum. (b) Wrong valuation, carbon leakage to other countries, lobbying, administrative cost.

items.stem: Extract: Scientists estimate the marginal external cost of carbon emissions in Umbria Nova at $50 per tonne. The government is debating a carbon tax of $30 per tonne, a cap-and-trade permit scheme, or stricter regulation of power stations. (a) Explain whether the proposed tax is likely to achieve the social optimum. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a cap-and-trade scheme sets the quantity of emissions.
items.answer: (a) Tax below MEC: output still above the optimum. (b) Vertical supply of permits at the cap; demand for permits from firms; price set by the market; firms with low abatement costs sell.

items.stem: Tradable pollution permits reduce pollution at the lowest total cost because
options: every firm must cut pollution by the same amount
firms that can cut pollution most cheaply do most of the abatement and sell their spare permits
permits are given only to the largest polluters
the government sets the price of each permit
items.answer: firms that can cut pollution most cheaply do most of the abatement and sell their spare permits
items.markingKey: Trading equalises marginal abatement cost across firms.

items.stem: In the market for plastic bags, demand is Qd = 330 − 2P and supply is Qs = 270 + 2P (Q in thousand units, P in $). The government imposes a specific tax of $8 per unit on producers. Calculate the equilibrium price before the tax.
Air quality in Bogotá has deteriorated sharply in recent years. Discuss whether tradable pollution permits are more effective than taxes in reducing pollution.
items.answer: Arguments for: Permits fix the quantity, reduce pollution at least cost, and the cap can be tightened. Arguments against / evaluation: Taxes give price certainty and revenue; permits can be over-allocated and prices volatile; monitoring needed for both; choice depends on the pollutant. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Extending property rights can reduce an externality because
options: it lowers the price of the good
the owner can charge for, or take legal action over, damage to their property
it forces firms to merge
it removes the need for any market
items.answer: the owner can charge for, or take legal action over, damage to their property
items.markingKey: Coase: clear rights allow bargaining to an efficient outcome.

items.stem: Explain two arguments for privatisation.
items.answer: Profit motive and competition improve efficiency (reduce X-inefficiency); access to private capital for investment; government revenue from sales; less political interference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why privatising a natural monopoly may not benefit consumers.
items.answer: It turns a public monopoly into a private one with an incentive to raise prices and restrict output; regulation is needed and may be captured.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: private monopoly; 1 mark: higher prices/need for regulation [2]

items.stem: Extract: Valdoria privatised its electricity generation company five years ago. Employment fell from 80 thousand to 64 thousand workers while output rose from 400 to 500 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 120. Explain why productivity may have risen after privatisation.
items.answer: Profit motive and shareholder pressure reduce X-inefficiency; investment from private capital; competition if the market was opened.

items.stem: Extract: Kestria privatised its telecommunications company five years ago. Employment fell from 60 thousand to 36 thousand workers while output rose from 500 to 625 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 112. (a) Explain why productivity may have risen after privatisation. (b) Explain what the change in the real price index suggests.
items.answer: (a) Profit motive and shareholder pressure reduce X-inefficiency; investment from private capital; competition if the market was opened. (b) Real prices rose, so efficiency gains were not passed on to consumers, possibly due to monopoly power.

items.stem: The government of Gorvania plans to sell its state-owned soft drinks company. Consider whether privatisation always improves economic efficiency.
items.answer: Arguments for: Profit motive, competition and private capital reduce X-inefficiency. Arguments against / evaluation: Private monopolies need regulation; quality and universal service may suffer; efficiency gains depend on competition, not ownership. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Explain why the Coase theorem is unlikely to solve pollution from a large city’s traffic.
items.answer: There are millions of affected people and polluters, so bargaining costs are huge; it is hard to identify who causes damage and enforce rights.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: many parties/high transaction costs; 1 mark: identification/enforcement [2]

items.stem: Extract: Valdoria privatised its telecommunications company five years ago. Employment fell from 120 thousand to 90 thousand workers while output rose from 600 to 660 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 105. (a) Calculate output per worker before and after privatisation and the percentage change. (b) Explain why productivity may have risen after privatisation.
items.answer: (a) 5 and 7.33 thousand units per worker; 46.7% (b) Profit motive and shareholder pressure reduce X-inefficiency; investment from private capital; competition if the market was opened.
items.markingKey: (a) output ÷ workers [2]; % change [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: An RPI − X price cap allows a regulated firm to raise its prices each year by
options: the rate of inflation plus X
whatever the firm chooses
the rate of inflation minus an efficiency factor X
X% regardless of inflation
items.answer: the rate of inflation minus an efficiency factor X
items.markingKey: E.g. inflation 5%, X = 2 → prices may rise 3%.

items.stem: Explain how an RPI − X price cap gives a monopoly an incentive to become more efficient.
items.answer: Prices must rise by less than inflation, so the firm can only keep its profit if it cuts costs by at least X% in real terms; any extra efficiency gains are kept as profit until the next review.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: real price falls; 1 mark: must cut costs; 1 mark: keeps extra gains [3]

items.stem: Explain two anti-competitive practices that competition authorities investigate.
items.answer: Price fixing by cartels; predatory pricing to drive out rivals; abuse of dominant position (exclusive dealing, refusal to supply); market sharing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: A regulator sets an RPI − X price cap on electricity distribution in Umbria Nova. The current average charge is $80, inflation (RPI) is 8% and X = 2. Calculate the maximum average charge allowed next year.

A regulator sets an RPI − X price cap on airport charges in Istrana. The current average charge is $50, inflation (RPI) is 8% and X = 1.5. The firm’s average cost is $40 now and is expected to be $42.77 next year. (a) Calculate the maximum charge next year. (b) Calculate the profit margin per unit now and next year. (c) Explain how the cap affects incentives and one weakness of this form of regulation.
items.answer: (a) $53.25 (b) now $10; next year $10.48 (c) The firm keeps any savings beyond X, so it has an incentive to cut costs; weaknesses: setting X needs good information, firms may cut quality, regulatory capture.
items.markingKey: (a) (8 − 1.5)% rise [2]; (b) price − average cost each year [2]; (c) incentive [1] and weakness [1].

items.stem: The competition authority of Istrana is investigating the hotel industry. (a) Explain the main aims of competition policy. (b) To what extent do you agree that competition policy always benefits consumers?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Prevents abuse of market power, collusion and harmful mergers, lowering prices. (b) Case for the view: Prevents abuse of market power, collusion and harmful mergers, lowering prices. Case against / evaluation: Blocking mergers may lose economies of scale and dynamic efficiency; investigations are costly and slow; global markets. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Explain how tradable pollution permits work.
items.answer: The government sets a cap on total emissions and issues permits; firms must hold permits for each tonne emitted. Firms with low abatement costs cut emissions and sell surplus permits to firms with high costs, so the cap is met at least cost; the cap can be tightened over time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cap; 1 mark: permits required; 1 mark: trading by cost [3]

items.stem: Extract: Scientists estimate the marginal external cost of carbon emissions in Selmaria at $60 per tonne. The government is debating a carbon tax of $120 per tonne, a cap-and-trade permit scheme, or stricter regulation of power stations. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a cap-and-trade scheme sets the quantity of emissions. (b) Explain one way in which this intervention could lead to government failure.
items.answer: (a) Vertical supply of permits at the cap; demand for permits from firms; price set by the market; firms with low abatement costs sell. (b) Wrong valuation, carbon leakage to other countries, lobbying, administrative cost.

items.stem: Government failure occurs when
options: government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than before
markets fail to provide public goods
the government runs a budget deficit
tax revenue falls
items.answer: government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources than before
items.markingKey: Intervention worsens welfare or costs more than it gains.

items.stem: Explain two causes of government failure.
items.answer: Imperfect information (wrong tax/subsidy levels); unintended consequences (black markets, evasion); administrative costs; political self-interest and short-termism; regulatory capture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why setting a tax higher than the marginal external cost could reduce welfare.
items.answer: Output falls below the social optimum, so units with MSB > MSC are no longer produced, creating a new welfare loss.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: output below optimum; 1 mark: welfare loss [2]

items.stem: A government in Quentara subsidises biofuel crops; farmers switch land from food, and food prices rise sharply. Which cause of government failure is illustrated?
options: Regulatory capture
Excessive administrative costs
Imperfect information / incorrect valuation
Unintended consequences
items.answer: Unintended consequences
items.markingKey: Unintended consequences.

items.stem: Rent controls in Kuala Lumpur lead landlords to sell flats, reducing the supply of rented housing. Which cause of government failure is illustrated?
options: Regulatory capture
Imperfect information / incorrect valuation
Unintended consequences
Political self-interest and short-termism
items.answer: Unintended consequences
items.markingKey: Unintended consequences.

items.stem: In Lunaria City, the demand for rented flats is Qd = 31,000 − 2P and supply is Qs = 29,000 + 2P, where P is monthly rent in $. The city sets a maximum rent of $300. Calculate the equilibrium rent, the quantity demanded and supplied at the maximum rent, and the shortage. Explain why this may be an example of government failure.
items.answer: Equilibrium rent $500, 30,000 flats. At $300: Qd = 30,400, Qs = 29,600, shortage = 800 flats. Government failure: fewer flats are available than before, queues and black markets appear and quality may fall, so the policy may harm the tenants it aims to help.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium 31,000 − 2P = 29,000 + 2P → P = 500 [1]; Qd and Qs at ceiling [2]; shortage 800 [1]; unintended consequences explained [1].

items.stem: The incidence of an indirect tax falls mainly on consumers when
options: demand is more elastic than supply
demand is perfectly elastic
demand is price inelastic relative to supply
supply is perfectly inelastic
items.answer: demand is price inelastic relative to supply
items.markingKey: The less elastic side bears more of the tax.

items.stem: The government of Calvania plans to subsidise electric buses in Kathmandu. Explain how the subsidy could improve the allocation of resources.
items.answer: Electric buses create external benefits (less pollution and congestion). The subsidy lowers the cost to operators, increasing supply and use towards the social optimum where MSB = MSC, reducing the welfare loss from under-consumption.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: positive externality identified; 1 mark: subsidy raises output to optimum [2]

items.stem: Two firms each emit pollution. Everline emits 100 tonnes and can cut emissions at a constant cost of $30 per tonne; Quarry Bay Ltd emits 100 tonnes with an abatement cost of $60 per tonne. The government wants a total cut of 80 tonnes. Calculate the total cost if (a) each firm must cut 40 tonnes, (b) tradable permits are issued so that the total cut is achieved at least cost. (c) Explain why the permit price would lie between $30 and $60 per tonne.
items.answer: (a) $3,600 (b) $2,400: Everline makes the whole cut; saving $1,200 (c) Quarry Bay Ltd will pay up to $60 (its abatement cost) for a permit rather than cut; Everline will sell for at least $30, so trade occurs between these prices.
items.markingKey: (a) 40×30 + 40×60 = $3,600 [2]; (b) low-cost firm abates 80 × 30 = $2,400 [2]; (c) willingness to pay vs accept [2].

the deregulation of financial markets
the transfer of firms from the private to the public sector
the transfer of ownership of assets or firms from the public sector to the private sector

items.stem: A factory upstream of a fish farm in Sundara pollutes the river, costing the fish farm $50,000 a year. The factory could install a filter for $30,000 a year. Explain, using the Coase theorem, how an efficient outcome could be reached if (a) the fish farm has the right to clean water, (b) the factory has the right to pollute.
items.answer: (a) The factory must stop polluting or compensate; filtering ($30,000) is cheaper than compensation ($50,000), so it installs the filter. (b) The fish farm will pay the factory up to $50,000 to install the $30,000 filter, so the filter is installed. Either way the efficient outcome (filter) is reached; only the distribution of costs differs.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [2]; conclusion on efficiency independent of rights [1]

items.stem: Regulatory capture occurs when
options: a regulator takes ownership of a firm
firms refuse to be regulated
consumers set prices
a regulator comes to act in the interests of the firms it regulates
items.answer: a regulator comes to act in the interests of the firms it regulates
items.markingKey: Close relationships, information asymmetry, revolving door.

items.stem: Fendaria bans the use of a pesticide that harms rivers. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a ban compared with a tax.
items.answer: Advantage: certain outcome, simple to understand, appropriate when damage is severe. Disadvantage: no revenue, no incentive for innovation beyond compliance, enforcement costs, may be inefficient if some use is socially worthwhile.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Three cement producers in Lunaria raised prices by exactly 12% on the same day and their market shares have not changed for six years. Analyse whether the competition authority should investigate them.
items.answer: Simultaneous identical price rises and stable shares suggest collusion (explicit or tacit), which raises price above competitive levels and causes allocative inefficiency. However, identical rises could reflect a common cost shock (energy prices) and price leadership; the authority needs evidence of agreement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: collusion signs; 1 mark: welfare effects; 1 mark: alternative explanation; 1 mark: judgement [4]

items.stem: Fenwick & Co, which has 70% of the hotel market in Westaria, offers big discounts to retailers that agree not to stock rival products. Analyse why this may be anti-competitive.
items.answer: Exclusive dealing raises barriers to entry and forecloses rivals’ access to outlets, entrenching dominance; in the long run prices may rise and choice and innovation fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: abuse of dominance; 1 mark: barrier to entry; 1 mark: consumer harm; 1 mark: development [4]

The government wants a total cut of 40 tonnes. Calculate the total cost if (a) each firm must cut 20 tonnes, (b) tradable permits are issued so that the total cut is achieved at least cost. (c) Explain why the permit price would lie between $50 and $60 per tonne.
items.answer: (a) $2,200 (b) $2,000: Ironleaf makes the whole cut; saving $200 (c) Silverline will pay up to $60 (its abatement cost) for a permit rather than cut; Ironleaf will sell for at least $50, so trade occurs between these prices.
items.markingKey: (a) 20×50 + 20×60 = $2,200 [2]; (b) low-cost firm abates 40 × 50 = $2,000 [2]; (c) willingness to pay vs accept [2].

items.stem: In the market for sugary drinks, demand is Qd = 345 − 3P and supply is Qs = 285 + 1P (Q in thousand units, P in $). The government imposes a specific tax of $8 per unit on producers. Calculate the equilibrium price before the tax.

Extract: Scientists estimate the marginal external cost of carbon emissions in Jovania at $40 per tonne. The government is debating a carbon tax of $120 per tonne, a cap-and-trade permit scheme, or stricter regulation of power stations. (a) Explain whether the proposed tax is likely to achieve the social optimum. (b) Explain one way in which this intervention could lead to government failure.
items.answer: (a) Tax above MEC: output would fall below the optimum (government failure). (b) Wrong valuation, carbon leakage to other countries, lobbying, administrative cost.

items.stem: Which is an argument for nationalisation of a natural monopoly?
options: It encourages competition between many firms
It always increases productive efficiency
The state can set price closer to marginal cost and serve unprofitable areas
It raises money for the government by selling shares
items.answer: The state can set price closer to marginal cost and serve unprofitable areas
items.markingKey: Public interest, universal service, control of strategic industries.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the Coase theorem is unlikely to solve pollution from a large city’s traffic. (b) Explain two arguments for privatisation.
items.answer: (a) There are millions of affected people and polluters, so bargaining costs are huge; it is hard to identify who causes damage and enforce rights. (b) Profit motive and competition improve efficiency (reduce X-inefficiency); access to private capital for investment; government revenue from sales; less political interference.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: many parties/high transaction costs; 1 mark: identification/enforcement [2] (b) 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Extract: Gorvania privatised its water company five years ago. Employment fell from 120 thousand to 90 thousand workers while output rose from 600 to 660 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 90. Explain what the change in the real price index suggests.
items.answer: Real prices fell, so consumers gained.

items.stem: Extract: Esteria privatised its water company five years ago. Employment fell from 60 thousand to 45 thousand workers while output rose from 400 to 440 million units. The real price index rose from 100 to 112. (a) Explain why productivity may have risen after privatisation. (b) Explain what the change in the real price index suggests.
items.answer: (a) Profit motive and shareholder pressure reduce X-inefficiency; investment from private capital; competition if the market was opened. (b) Real prices rose, so efficiency gains were not passed on to consumers, possibly due to monopoly power.

items.stem: The government of Gorvania plans to sell its state-owned cinema company. ‘Privatisation always improves economic efficiency.’ Evaluate this statement.
items.answer: Arguments for: Profit motive, competition and private capital reduce X-inefficiency. Arguments against / evaluation: Private monopolies need regulation; quality and universal service may suffer; efficiency gains depend on competition, not ownership. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Competition authorities are most likely to block a merger that
options: joins firms in unrelated industries with small shares
lowers prices for consumers
creates a firm with 5% market share
would create a dominant firm with a large market share and high barriers to entry
items.answer: would create a dominant firm with a large market share and high barriers to entry
items.markingKey: Concern: substantial lessening of competition.

items.stem: The government of Tarvia plans to subsidise electric buses in Seoul. Explain how the subsidy could improve the allocation of resources.
items.answer: Electric buses create external benefits (less pollution and congestion). The subsidy lowers the cost to operators, increasing supply and use towards the social optimum where MSB = MSC, reducing the welfare loss from under-consumption.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: positive externality identified; 1 mark: subsidy raises output to optimum [2]

items.stem: A regulator sets an RPI − X price cap on rail fares in Umbria Nova. The current average charge is $60, inflation (RPI) is 5% and X = 1. Calculate the maximum average charge allowed next year.

A regulator sets an RPI − X price cap on water in Rovania. The current average charge is $40, inflation (RPI) is 4% and X = 3. The firm’s average cost is $28 now and is expected to be $27.96 next year. (a) Calculate the maximum charge next year. (b) Calculate the profit margin per unit now and next year. (c) Explain how the cap affects incentives and one weakness of this form of regulation.
items.answer: (a) $40.40 (b) now $12; next year $12.44 (c) The firm keeps any savings beyond X, so it has an incentive to cut costs; weaknesses: setting X needs good information, firms may cut quality, regulatory capture.
items.markingKey: (a) (4 − 3)% rise [2]; (b) price − average cost each year [2]; (c) incentive [1] and weakness [1].

items.stem: (a) Explain how an RPI − X price cap works. (b) Consider whether regulation of monopolies is more effective than breaking them up.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Price caps and regulation keep economies of scale while protecting consumers. (b) Case for the view: Price caps and regulation keep economies of scale while protecting consumers. Case against / evaluation: Regulatory capture, information asymmetry, cost of regulation; breaking up may increase competition but lose economies of scale; depends on natural monopoly. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how an indirect tax can correct a negative production externality. (b) Explain two problems a government faces in setting the correct tax on pollution.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: MPC below MSC by MEC; demand = MSB. Market output Q1 where MPC = MSB. A tax equal to MEC at Q* shifts MPC up to MSC (MPC + tax), so output falls to Q* where MSC = MSB and price rises; the welfare loss triangle is removed and tax revenue is raised. (b) Difficulty measuring the marginal external cost; MEC varies by location and time; inelastic demand means output falls little; political pressure; firms may relocate.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: curves; 1 mark: tax shifts supply up by MEC; 1 mark: new output Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss eliminated [4] (b) 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain two problems a government faces in setting the correct tax on pollution. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how an indirect tax can correct a negative production externality.
items.answer: (a) Difficulty measuring the marginal external cost; MEC varies by location and time; inelastic demand means output falls little; political pressure; firms may relocate. (b) Diagram: MPC below MSC by MEC; demand = MSB. Market output Q1 where MPC = MSB. A tax equal to MEC at Q* shifts MPC up to MSC (MPC + tax), so output falls to Q* where MSC = MSB and price rises; the welfare loss triangle is removed and tax revenue is raised.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4] (b) 1 mark: curves; 1 mark: tax shifts supply up by MEC; 1 mark: new output Q*; 1 mark: welfare loss eliminated [4]

items.stem: In Port Kestria, the demand for rented flats is Qd = 31,200 − 3P and supply is Qs = 28,800 + 3P, where P is monthly rent in $. The city sets a maximum rent of $200. Calculate the equilibrium rent, the quantity demanded and supplied at the maximum rent, and the shortage. Explain why this may be an example of government failure.
items.answer: Equilibrium rent $400, 30,000 flats. At $200: Qd = 30,600, Qs = 29,400, shortage = 1,200 flats. Government failure: fewer flats are available than before, queues and black markets appear and quality may fall, so the policy may harm the tenants it aims to help.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium 31,200 − 3P = 28,800 + 3P → P = 400 [1]; Qd and Qs at ceiling [2]; shortage 1,200 [1]; unintended consequences explained [1].

items.stem: Several recent interventions in Pelora, including rent controls and fuel subsidies, have been criticised. (a) Explain what is meant by government failure, using examples. (b) Consider whether government failure means that governments should not intervene in markets.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Imperfect information, unintended consequences and political motives can make outcomes worse. (b) Case for the view: Imperfect information, unintended consequences and political motives can make outcomes worse. Case against / evaluation: Market failure may be larger; better information and design reduce failure; compare costs of intervention with costs of market failure. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.
